title: How would you design an OTP service that survives a login spike (50k RPS onto a 10k/min SMS provider) — the key fix is the "Resend" button re-sends the EXISTING valid OTP instead of generating a new one, plus multi-level rate limiting, queue buffering with TTL/priority to absorb the spike, provider failover, and TOTP/email as provider-independent fallbacks?
shortTitle: How would you design an OTP service that survives a login spike

s1_definition.profdef: An OTP service that survives a spike, where request rate far exceeds the SMS provider's capacity, is built to minimise provider calls and absorb bursts rather than forward them. The key fix is that the Resend button re-sends the existing still-valid OTP instead of generating and sending a new one, which removes the retry-storm amplification where impatient users multiply the load. On top of that it applies multi-level rate limiting at the user, IP, provider, and global levels, buffers requests in a queue with a time-to-live and priority so the spike is smoothed to the provider's sustainable rate, fails over across multiple SMS providers each with its own token-bucket limit, and offers provider-independent fallbacks like time-based one-time passwords or email so that authentication is still possible when SMS capacity is saturated.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's branch can only hand out ten thousand paper tokens per minute, but on a busy morning fifty thousand customers a second rush the counter demanding one. If every impatient customer who already has a valid token keeps re-asking for a new one, the counter is instantly overwhelmed by people who do not even need a new token. The single biggest fix is a rule: if you already hold a valid token, the clerk just re-hands you the same one, not a fresh one. Then the branch adds crowd control, nobody gets more than three tokens in five minutes, suspicious groups are slowed, and a waiting line with a buffer feeds the counter at exactly its safe pace. If the main token printer jams, a backup printer and even a mobile-app token that needs no printer at all keep things moving.
s1_definition.oneliner: Survive an OTP spike by making Resend re-send the existing valid OTP instead of a new one, then add multi-level rate limiting, a TTL-and-priority queue to smooth the burst to the provider's rate, multi-provider failover with a token bucket per provider, and provider-independent TOTP or email fallbacks.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An OTP service that survives a spike, where request rate far exceeds the SMS provider's capacity, is built to minimise provider calls and absorb bursts rather than forward them. The key fix is that the Resend button re-sends the existing still-valid OTP instead of generating and sending a new one, which removes the retry-storm amplification where impatient users multiply the load. On top of that it applies multi-level rate limiting at the user, IP, provider, and global levels, buffers requests in a queue with a time-to-live and priority so the spike is smoothed to the provider's sustainable rate, fails over across multiple SMS providers each with its own token-bucket limit, and offers provider-independent fallbacks like time-based one-time passwords or email so that authentication is still possible when SMS capacity is saturated.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's branch can only hand out ten thousand paper tokens per minute, but on a busy morning fifty thousand customers a second rush the counter demanding one. If every impatient customer who already has a valid token keeps re-asking for a new one, the counter is instantly overwhelmed by people who do not even need a new token. The single biggest fix is a rule: if you already hold a valid token, the clerk just re-hands you the same one, not a fresh one. Then the branch adds crowd control, nobody gets more than three tokens in five minutes, suspicious groups are slowed, and a waiting line with a buffer feeds the counter at exactly its safe pace. If the main token printer jams, a backup printer and even a mobile-app token that needs no printer at all keep things moving.

**One line to remember:** Survive an OTP spike by making Resend re-send the existing valid OTP instead of a new one, then add multi-level rate limiting, a TTL-and-priority queue to smooth the burst to the provider's rate, multi-provider failover with a token bucket per provider, and provider-independent TOTP or email fallbacks.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with the core problem: a demand-supply mismatch. The service receives a huge request rate during a spike, far more than the SMS provider can physically deliver, so you cannot simply forward every request; you must reduce the number of provider calls and pace the rest. The single most effective reduction comes from killing retry amplification, which is where the Resend fix lives.

The Resend fix is the headline, so understand the amplification it removes. Normally a user requests an OTP, waits, gets impatient when SMS is slow, and taps Resend, often several times, and each tap, if it generates and sends a brand-new OTP, multiplies the provider load by the number of impatient taps. During a spike this amplification is exactly what pushes a merely heavy load into a catastrophic one. The fix is that Resend re-sends the existing OTP if it is still valid: when a user requests an OTP you store it with its expiry, and when Resend arrives you check for a live OTP for that user and, if one exists, re-send that same code rather than minting a new one. This means a user who taps Resend five times generates at most the original provider calls plus a few cheap re-sends that can themselves be rate-limited, instead of five full new generations. It also improves user experience because the code they may already have received still works. This one change often cuts provider load dramatically because retry storms are the dominant source of amplification.

Multi-level rate limiting protects at different scopes, because a single limiter cannot address every abuse and load pattern. A per-user limit, for example three OTPs in five minutes, stops one user, or one impatient person, from consuming disproportionate capacity. A per-IP limit with escalation to a CAPTCHA catches a single source generating many requests across many accounts, which is the signature of an attacker or a broken client. A per-provider limit, implemented as a token bucket sized to that provider's contractual rate, ensures you never exceed what a provider will accept, which both avoids rejections and enables clean failover. A global cap protects the whole system and downstream from a flood larger than you can ever serve, shedding or queueing excess. These layers compose so that each catches a different pattern, and the per-provider token bucket in particular is what makes failover work, because it tells you precisely when a provider is tapped out.

Queue buffering with time-to-live and priority absorbs the burst and smooths it to the sustainable rate. Instead of calling the provider synchronously on the request path, you enqueue send jobs and have workers consume them at a rate matched to the provider's capacity, so a fifty-thousand-per-second spike lands in the queue and drains to the provider at its ten-thousand-per-minute limit without dropping everything. The time-to-live matters because an OTP is useless after it expires, so a send job that has waited past the OTP's validity is discarded rather than sending a stale code, which also naturally sheds load during extreme spikes. Priority matters because not all OTPs are equal: a high-value action like a large transfer or a password reset should jump ahead of routine logins, so you use a priority queue that serves critical sends first when capacity is scarce.

Provider failover keeps delivery flowing when one provider degrades. You integrate multiple SMS providers, each with its own token bucket reflecting its rate limit, and you order them primary, secondary, tertiary. When the primary's bucket is empty or it starts returning errors or timing out, you fail over to the next provider whose bucket still has tokens, rather than hammering the exhausted one. Health checks and the circuit-breaker idea apply here: a failing provider is marked unhealthy and skipped until it recovers. Because each provider has its own bucket, failover is clean, you route to a provider that can actually accept the send instead of retrying against one that cannot.

Provider-independent fallbacks remove the single point of failure that is SMS itself. A time-based one-time password, TOTP, is generated on the user's device from a shared secret and a clock, so it needs no network call and no SMS at all, which means during a spike users with TOTP set up can authenticate with zero provider load. Email OTP is another channel with different capacity and provider, so when SMS is saturated you can route some traffic to email. Offering these fallbacks means the system can still authenticate people even when every SMS provider is at capacity, which is the ultimate resilience.

Senior nuances worth stating: store OTPs in a fast store like Redis with the expiry as the time-to-live so validity and the Resend check are cheap; make the whole send path idempotent per request so retries do not double-send; combine the Resend fix with a short cooldown so even re-sends are paced; prefer shedding expired queue jobs over sending stale codes; size each provider's token bucket to its contract and monitor bucket depletion as an early warning; and treat TOTP as the strategic long-term answer because it decouples you from SMS economics and latency entirely. The through-line is reduce provider calls first, then pace and route what remains, then fall back to channels that need no provider.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — During a festival promotion, fifty thousand customers a second tried to log in to National Bank of India, and the SMS provider could only deliver ten thousand a minute, so OTPs were not arriving and users kept tapping Resend, each tap generating a brand-new OTP and multiplying the load. This is exactly the retry-storm amplification, solved by making Resend re-send the existing valid OTP instead of a new one.

Problem 2 — A single script was requesting OTPs for thousands of accounts from one IP. This is exactly the abuse pattern that a single limiter misses, solved by multi-level rate limiting with a per-IP limit escalating to CAPTCHA alongside the per-user limit.

Problem 3 — The provider could not take the whole burst at once, and when it was saturated the system needed another way. This is exactly the queue-plus-failover-plus-fallback problem, solved by a TTL-and-priority queue draining at the provider's rate, failover to a second provider with its own token bucket, and TOTP as a provider-independent fallback.

Our mini-project builds an OTP service core. The code generates and stores an OTP with expiry, makes Resend re-send the existing valid code, applies per-user and per-provider token-bucket limits, enqueues sends with TTL and priority, fails over between two providers, and verifies a TOTP fallback. The demo logs Rajesh requesting then resending an OTP during a simulated spike.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh requests an OTP, then taps Resend three times during a spike, an abusive IP requests OTPs for twenty-five accounts, and finally a TOTP fallback is verified.

Step 1: Rajesh's first request passes the per-user and per-IP limits. The store generates a six-digit code and saves it with a five-minute time-to-live. The router enqueues a send, which drains to the primary provider within its token bucket. One provider call was made.

Step 2: Rajesh gets impatient and taps Resend. The service looks up his existing OTP, finds it still valid, and re-sends that same code rather than generating a new one, after passing a short cooldown. This is the key fix: the Resend does not mint a new OTP, so it adds at most a cheap, paced re-send instead of a full new generation.

Step 3: Rajesh taps Resend two more times. The cooldown paces them, and each time the existing valid code is re-sent, never a new one. Across four taps the system generated exactly one OTP, whereas the naive design would have generated four, which during a fifty-thousand-per-second spike is the difference between survivable and catastrophic load.

Step 4: The abusive IP requests OTPs for twenty-five different users. The per-user limits are fine since each user is distinct, but the per-IP counter crosses its threshold of twenty, so further requests from that IP are blocked and escalated to a CAPTCHA. This catches the attack that a per-user limit alone would miss.

Step 5: As legitimate spike traffic accumulates, the primary provider's token bucket depletes. When it empties, the router fails over cleanly to the secondary provider, which has its own bucket with tokens, rather than hammering the exhausted primary. If both buckets empty, sends are queued with TTL so stale ones are shed, or routed to email.

Step 6: A TOTP fallback is verified for Rajesh. Because TOTP is computed from a shared secret and the clock on the device, it needs no SMS and no provider call at all, so it verifies instantly and adds zero provider load. This is the ultimate resilience: authentication continues even when every SMS provider is saturated.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:12:20 INFO    generated OTP for RAJESH (valid 300s)
2026-10-24 15:12:20 INFO    RESEND existing OTP for RAJESH (no amplification)
2026-10-24 15:12:20 WARNING resend cooldown for RAJESH
2026-10-24 15:12:20 WARNING resend cooldown for RAJESH
2026-10-24 15:12:20 WARNING per-IP limit → CAPTCHA for 66.66.66.66
2026-10-24 15:12:20 INFO    TOTP fallback verify for Rajesh = true (zero provider load)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Login spike: 50k RPS  ▶  SMS provider cap: 10k/min  (huge mismatch)

  OTP request (user, ip)
    │
    ▼
  Multi-level rate limiting
    ├─ per-user (3/5min)      ─ over? → reject
    ├─ per-IP (20/5min)       ─ over? → CAPTCHA   ← catches 1 IP, many accounts
    ├─ global cap             ─ over? → shed
    ▼
  OtpStore.generate() → code + TTL 5min (Redis)
    │
    ▼
  Priority+TTL queue ───drains at provider rate──▶ ProviderRouter
    │ (50k/s absorbed; stale jobs dropped)          ├─ SMS-PRIMARY bucket (10k/min)
    │                                               │   empty? FAILOVER ▼
    │                                               ├─ SMS-SECONDARY bucket (5k/min)
    │                                               │   empty? ▼
    │                                               └─ email fallback / TTL-shed

  ── RESEND (the key fix) ──
  Resend tap → OtpStore.currentValid(user)
    ├─ valid OTP exists → RE-SEND SAME code (cooldown-paced)  ← NO new generation
    └─ expired → generate new
  effect: 4 taps = 1 generation (not 4) → kills retry-storm amplification

  ── Provider-independent fallback ──
  TOTP: device + shared secret + clock → verify with ZERO SMS calls
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
An OTP service that survives a login spike is fundamentally a demand-supply mismatch problem: requests arrive far faster than the SMS provider can deliver, so I cannot forward every request and must reduce provider calls and pace the rest. The single most effective fix, and the one I lead with, is that the Resend button re-sends the existing still-valid OTP instead of generating a new one. The reason is retry-storm amplification: when SMS is slow, impatient users tap Resend repeatedly, and if each tap mints and sends a fresh OTP, the provider load multiplies by the number of taps, which turns a heavy spike into a catastrophic one. By storing each OTP with its expiry and re-sending the same code on Resend, a user who taps five times generates at most one OTP plus a few cheap, cooldown-paced re-sends, which typically cuts provider load dramatically.

On top of that I apply multi-level rate limiting because one limiter cannot catch every pattern. A per-user limit stops one person consuming disproportionate capacity, a per-IP limit escalating to CAPTCHA catches one source requesting OTPs across many accounts, a per-provider token bucket ensures I never exceed a provider's contractual rate, and a global cap protects everything downstream. The per-provider token bucket is especially important because it tells me exactly when a provider is tapped out, which is what makes failover clean.

I absorb the burst with a queue that has a time-to-live and priority. Instead of calling the provider synchronously, I enqueue send jobs and drain them at the provider's sustainable rate, so a fifty-thousand-per-second spike lands in the queue and flows out at the provider's limit. The time-to-live means a job that has waited past the OTP's validity is discarded rather than sending a stale code, which naturally sheds load, and priority means a high-value action like a large transfer jumps ahead of routine logins when capacity is scarce. I integrate multiple providers ordered primary, secondary, tertiary, each with its own token bucket, and fail over to the next provider that still has tokens when one is empty or unhealthy, instead of hammering an exhausted one. Finally I offer provider-independent fallbacks: a time-based one-time password generated on the device needs no SMS and no network call, so it adds zero provider load, and email is a separate channel with different capacity, so authentication continues even when every SMS provider is saturated.

On my project at National Bank of India a festival promotion produced exactly this spike, and the Resend fix was transformative on its own, because the retry storm had been the dominant load, and making Resend re-send the existing code collapsed four or five generations per user down to one. We added per-user and per-IP limits that stopped an abusive script, a TTL-and-priority queue that smoothed the burst and shed expired sends, failover between two SMS providers each with its own token bucket, and TOTP for customers who had enrolled it, which let them log in with no provider involvement at all. The through-line I stress is reduce provider calls first, then pace and route what remains, then fall back to channels that need no provider.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I survive an OTP spike by making Resend re-send the existing valid OTP to kill retry-storm amplification, then layering multi-level rate limiting, a TTL-and-priority queue that smooths the burst to the provider's rate, multi-provider failover with a token bucket per provider, and provider-independent TOTP or email fallbacks so authentication keeps working even when SMS is fully saturated.
